A QUICK-LEARNING HANDBOOK System Design Playbook How real systems work, and the patterns behind them: security, storage, caching, networking, real-time and reliability, explained for backend engineers. SEVEN PARTS · 26 CHAPTERS BEFORE YOU START How to read this book Every chapter has the same layout, so you always know where to look: The idea — the whole chapter in one sentence. How it works — five steps, left to right. Remember — three points for revision and interviews. Deep dive — the reasoning, trade-offs, failure modes and a Java/Spring angle. Skip it when you only need a refresher. Where the topics come from The chapters on password storage, JWT, Apple Pay, AirTag, S3, Uber, YouTube/Vitess, Lambda, Figma, Stripe, Meta, Tinder, micro frontends and DNS cover the topics of Neo Kim's System Design Playbook cheat sheets. All explanations here are written fresh, and the other chapters add the surrounding concepts: replication and sharding, caching, load balancing, real-time channels, resilience, event-driven reliability and a quick-reference part. A note on accuracy These are simplified summaries of publicly described designs. Where a company has not published details, the text describes the general technique. Check version-specific behaviour against current official documentation before using it in production.

01 How Databases Store Passwords Securely THE IDEA Never store the password. Store a slow, salted fingerprint of it. HOW IT WORKS 1 Password User submits it 2 Salt + slow hash Random per-user value added 3 Store hash & salt Only the fingerprint is kept 4 Re-hash on login Same salt + params used again 5 Compare Constant-time match REMEMBER Store a salted, slow hash. Never the password. Use Argon2id or bcrypt; never plain SHA-256. Spring: DelegatingPasswordEncoder lets you migrate algorithms. DEEP DIVE A database that holds plaintext passwords turns every breach into a catastrophe. The standard defence is to store a one-way fingerprint instead: a hash cannot be reversed, so the server can check a password without ever keeping it. Why a plain hash is not enough Attackers precompute hashes of common passwords (a rainbow table) and simply look stolen hashes up. Fast general-purpose hashes such as SHA-256 also let a GPU test billions of guesses per second. Two ingredients fix this: Salt — a unique random value per user, stored next to the hash. Identical passwords then produce different hashes and precomputed tables become useless. Work factor — a deliberately slow, tunable algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id, PBKDF2) so each guess costs real CPU time or memory. Login flow Look up the user and read the stored salt, parameters and hash. Hash the submitted password with the same salt and parameters. Compare the two values in constant time; grant access only if they match. ALGORITHM STRENGTH NOTE Argon2id Memory-hard, resists GPU/ASIC Current first choice in OWASP guidance bcrypt Mature, CPU-hard 72-byte input limit; cost 10-12 typical scrypt Memory-hard Good alternative; harder to tune PBKDF2 FIPS-friendly Needs high iteration counts day. @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(); } // encoder.encode(raw) -> "{bcrypt}$2a$10$..." // encoder.matches(raw, stored) TRADE-OFF A slow hash also slows your login endpoint. Rate-limit logins, and tune the cost so one hash takes roughly 100–300 ms on production hardware. An optional pepper (a secret kept outside the database, e.g. in a KMS) adds protection if only the DB leaks.

02 How JWT Works THE IDEA A signed, self-contained token that lets servers stay stateless. HOW IT WORKS 1 Login User authenticates 2 Server signs JWT Header + payload + signature 3 Client stores it Browser cookie or app storage 4 Sends on each call Authorization header each time 5 Server verifies signature No session lookup needed REMEMBER A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Keep secrets out. Short expiry + refresh rotation; pin the algorithm. Stateless scale costs instant revocation. DEEP DIVE A JSON Web Token carries the user's identity and claims inside the token itself. The server signs it; any service that can verify the signature can trust the claims without a session lookup. That is why JWTs suit horizontally scaled and microservice systems. Structure Three Base64URL parts joined by dots: header (algorithm, key id), payload (claims such as sub , exp , iss , aud , roles) and signature. The payload is encoded, not encrypted — never put secrets in it. SIGNING WHO CAN VERIFY USE WHEN HS256 (shared Anyone holding the secret, who can One service signs and verifies secret) also forge RS256 / ES256 (key Anyone with the public key; only Many services verify; publish keys pair) issuer signs via JWKS Pitfalls that cause real incidents Accepting alg: none or letting the token choose the algorithm. Pin the expected algorithm server-side. it expires, so keep it to minutes. No revocation story. Use short expiry, refresh-token rotation and a jti denylist. Keeping tokens in localStorage (XSS-readable); prefer HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookies. TRADE-OFF Statelessness costs instant revocation. If you must cut users off in seconds, use opaque tokens with introspection or a denylist.

03 How Apple Pay Works THE IDEA Your card number never reaches the merchant; a device-bound token does. HOW IT WORKS 1 Add card Card sent to the network once 2 Network issues token (DAN) Token tied to this one device 3 Stored in Secure Element Secure Element holds the key 4 Tap: one-time cryptogram One-time code for this payment 5 Network validates Network recomputes and approves REMEMBER Merchants see a token, never the card number. A cryptogram works once, for one transaction. Pattern: swap a real secret for a scoped stand-in. DEEP DIVE Apple Pay is a case study in tokenization. When you add a card, the card details go to the card network (via the issuer), which returns a Device Account Number, a token that stands in for the card and is bound to that one device. Apple does not keep the real number on the phone or its servers. What happens at the terminal The phone talks to the reader over NFC and receives the transaction details (amount, merchant, a nonce). The Secure Element, an isolated tamper-resistant chip, produces a cryptogram: a one- time code computed from the token's key and those transaction details. Biometric approval gates this step. Only the token and the cryptogram travel onward. The merchant never sees the card number. The network recomputes the cryptogram with its copy of the key. A match proves the genuine device authorised this transaction, and the issuer then approves or declines. Why this design is strong Replay is useless. A cryptogram is valid for one transaction only. Breach containment. A merchant database leak exposes tokens that cannot be used anywhere else. Device binding. A stolen token without the Secure Element's key cannot generate valid cryptograms. Revocation is cheap. The issuer can disable one token without reissuing the card. TA K E AWAY The pattern generalises: replace a high-value secret with a low-value, scoped, single-use stand-in, and keep the real secret in the smallest possible trusted boundary. Payment gateways use the same idea for card-on-file tokens.

04 How Apple AirTag Works THE IDEA Crowd-sourced, end-to-end encrypted location tracking over Bluetooth. HOW IT WORKS 1 Tag broadcasts BLE Tag advertises a rotating key 2 Nearby phone hears it Any passing phone can listen 3 Encrypts location to tag key Encrypted to the tag's public key 4 Uploads to server Blob stored under a derived id 5 Owner decrypts Only the owner holds the key REMEMBER No GPS: other people's phones relay the location. Public-key encryption keeps Apple blind to it. Rotating IDs stop long-term tracking. DEEP DIVE An AirTag has no GPS and no internet connection. It is a tiny Bluetooth Low Energy beacon that relies on other people's devices to carry its location to the cloud. The design goal is that Apple can relay the data but cannot read it. The protocol in outline When the owner pairs the tag, a key pair is generated and the private key stays with the owner's devices. The tag broadcasts a public key over BLE, a few times per second. The advertised key rotates on a schedule, so a passive observer cannot follow one tag forever. Any nearby participating device hears the broadcast, gets its own location, and encrypts that location with the broadcast public key. It uploads the encrypted blob, indexed by a value derived from the public key, over HTTPS. The owner's device derives the same lookup values, fetches the blobs, and decrypts them with the private key. Design lessons Public-key encryption makes the relay blind. The finder's phone can encrypt but never decrypt. Rotating identifiers trade lookup convenience for privacy. Low-power budgets shape everything: no GPS, tiny payloads, infrequent advertising. Abuse is part of the design. Anti-stalking alerts exist because a tracker that follows you is a threat model, not an edge case. TA K E AWAY When a system must be reachable but not trusted with data, encrypt at the edge to a key the server never holds, and make identifiers unlinkable over time. 05 How Amazon S3 Works THE IDEA An object store built from many small services, a metadata index and a lot of disks. HOW IT WORKS 1 PUT object Client uploads to an endpoint 2 Front -end & auth Auth, then a key lookup 3 Metadata (key → location) Index maps key to location 4 Data nodes store bytes Bytes live on many disks 5 Return success Confirmed after storing REMEMBER Index (metadata) and bytes scale separately. Flat keys, not folders; parallel disks give throughput. Pre-signed URLs let clients upload directly. DEEP DIVE S3 stores objects (a blob plus metadata) in flat buckets. There is no real directory tree; a key like logs/2026/11/app.log is just a string. That simplicity is what lets it scale to trillions of objects. Separate the index from the bytes A request is handled by a fleet of stateless front-end services. They authenticate the caller, consult a metadata subsystem (a replicated key-value index that maps a key to where its data lives), and read or write to a separate storage layer of disk servers. Splitting the two lets each scale on its own axis: index size and request rate on one side, raw capacity and throughput on the other. Choices worth noticing Commodity hard disks for cost, with software providing the reliability. Sequentialfriendly on-disk layouts hide the seek penalty. Log-structured storage on each disk (AWS describes a custom store called ShardStore) so writes append rather than update in place. Parallelism — one object spans many disks, so reads pull from several at once. Erasure coding instead of full copies to cut storage overhead (next chapter). Strong read-after-write consistency since 2020, for new objects and overwrites. Using it well Spread key prefixes sensibly; S3 scales request rate per prefix. Use multipart upload for large objects, with parallel parts and retry per part. Use pre-signed URLs so clients upload directly and your service never proxies bytes. IN SPRING Prefer the AWS SDK v2 S3Client / S3TransferManager , or Spring Cloud AWS S3Template . Generate a pre-signed PUT URL in your API and let the browser or mobile app upload straight to S3.

06 How S3 Achieves 11 Nines of Durability THE IDEA Erasure coding, checksums everywhere, and relentless repair. HOW IT WORKS 1 Split into shards Cut into data shards 2 Add parity shards Compute extra shards 3 Spread across failure domains Different disks, racks, sites 4 Verify with checksums Checksums catch corruption 5 Detect failure → repair Rebuild fast from the rest REMEMBER Erasure coding: 10+4 shards survives 4 losses at 40% overhead. Checksums end to end; verify before acknowledging. Short repair time matters as much as copies. DEEP DIVE “Eleven nines” (99.999999999%) is a durability target, meaning the chance of losing a given object in a year is vanishingly small. It is not magic; it comes from layering several techniques and operating them with discipline. Erasure coding Instead of storing three full copies (200% overhead), data is split into k data shards and m parity shards computed with Reed-Solomon style codes. Any k of the k+m shards can rebuild the object. You survive several simultaneous losses at far lower storage cost than replication. SCHEME OVERHEAD SURVIVES TRADE-OFF 3x replication 200% 2 lost copies Simple, fast reads, costly Erasure code (e.g. 40% Any 4 lost CPU on encode/repair, more IO to 10+4) shards rebuild The supporting cast Failure domains. Shards land on different disks, racks and facilities with independent power and networking. Checksums end to end. Verified on upload, on every stored shard and again on read, so silent corruption (bit rot) is caught. Sending the checksum as an HTTP trailer lets large streams be verified without buffering. Verify before acknowledging. A write is confirmed only after the stored shards are checked. Fast, continuous repair. Durability depends on how quickly lost shards are rebuilt, because the risk window is the time spent degraded. Spare capacity on every disk keeps repair throughput high, and repair capacity is scaled from observed failure rates. Human safeguards. Versioning, backups and a durability review for risky changes. TA K E AWAY Durability = independent failure domains × short repair window × constant verification.

07 How YouTube Scales MySQL with Vitess THE IDEA A sharding and connection-management layer that makes many MySQLs look like one. HOW IT WORKS 1 App sends SQL App sends normal SQL 2 vtgate (proxy) parses & routes Proxy parses and routes 3 vttablet (sidecar) guards MySQL Sidecar guards each MySQL 4 Right shard executes Query hits the right shard 5 Topology in metadata store Shard map in a small store REMEMBER Keep MySQL; add a routing and protection layer. Pooling and query limits protect the primaries. Shard key choice decides if queries stay single-shard. DEEP DIVE As traffic grew, YouTube kept MySQL but added a layer above it. That layer, Vitess, was written in Go, open-sourced, and now underpins many large deployments. The idea: keep the proven storage engine, move scaling concerns into a purpose-built middle tier. Main components VTGate — a stateless proxy that speaks the MySQL protocol, parses queries, and routes or scatter-gathers them to the right shards. It also pools connections. VTTablet — a sidecar next to each MySQL instance. It enforces query limits, rewrites risky queries (for example adding a LIMIT ), and deduplicates identical in-flight reads so a hot row cannot cause a stampede. Topology service — a small strongly consistent store (etcd, ZooKeeper) holding shard maps and tablet state. VSchema — declares the sharding key and how tables are distributed. Why it works Connection pooling. MySQL handles thousands of connections poorly; the proxy multiplexes many clients onto few backend connections. Query protection. One runaway query is killed or bounded before it takes down a primary. Resharding online. Data can be split or merged while serving traffic. Replicas for reads and automated failover for availability. TRADE-OFF Cross-shard joins, transactions and unique constraints become expensive or limited. Choose a shard key that keeps most queries on one shard, and accept eventual or twophase semantics for the rest. If you are on managed MySQL, PlanetScale is Vitess as a service.

08 How Figma Scaled Postgres THE IDEA A scaling ladder: bigger box, replicas, cache, pooling, vertical then horizontal partitioning. HOW IT WORKS 1 Scale up Bigger instance 2 Read replicas + cache Replicas and a cache 3 PgBouncer pooling Pool connections 4 Vertical partition by domain Split tables by domain 5 Horizontal shard by key Split one table by key REMEMBER Climb the cheap steps first; shard last. Pooling and caching postpone sharding for years. Pick a high-cardinality, even shard key. DEEP DIVE Figma's journey is a textbook example of doing the cheap thing first. They stayed on PostgreSQL and climbed a ladder, only reaching for sharding when simpler steps ran out. Scale up. A larger instance buys time at almost no engineering cost. Read replicas absorb read traffic and give failover capacity. Beware replication lag for read-your-writes. Caching in front of the database removes the hottest reads entirely. Connection pooling (PgBouncer) prevents connection starvation, since each Postgres connection is a process. Vertical partitioning moves whole tables or domains onto separate databases, so one noisy feature cannot starve another. Horizontal sharding splits a single huge table by key across many databases. It brings routing logic, hard cross-shard queries and migration risk. Practical points Pick a shard key with high cardinality and even spread (a tenant or file id, not a timestamp). Build a logical sharding layer before the physical one, so you can roll back. Move data with dual writes, backfill and verification, then cut over per shard. Tables that join frequently should share a shard key to stay co-located. CHALLENGE TO THE USUAL INSTINCT Most teams shard too early. A properly indexed, well-pooled Postgres with replicas and a cache carries a surprising amount of load. Shard when write throughput or dataset size, not read volume, is the proven bottleneck.

09 Replication, Sharding and Consistency THE IDEA The vocabulary behind every database scaling decision. HOW IT WORKS 1 Replicate for availability Copies for availability 2 Shard for capacity Split data for capacity 3 Choose consistency level Pick how fresh reads must be 4 Plan for failure Design the failure path REMEMBER Replicate first, shard last. Consistent hashing moves ~1/N keys on resize. B-tree for reads; LSM for heavy writes. DEEP DIVE Replication MODEL HOW GOOD FOR RISK Single leader One writer, followers copy Most OLTP Failover, lag Multi-leader Writers in several regions Geo-writes Conflict resolution Leaderless Write W, read R of N High availability (Dynamo, Stale reads if (quorum) Cassandra) W+R≤N Sharding strategies Range — ordered, good for scans, prone to hot ranges. Hash — even spread, no range scans. Consistent hashing — adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of keys; virtual nodes smooth load. Directory — flexible, but a new dependency. Consistency spectrum Linearizable (behaves like one copy) → sequential → causal → read-your-writes / monotonic reads → eventual. Stronger guarantees cost latency and availability. CAP says that during a network partition you must choose consistency or availability; PACELC adds that even without a partition you trade latency for consistency. Indexes: B-tree vs LSM B-TREE (POSTGRES, MYSQL INNODB) LSM-TREE (CASSANDRA, ROCKSDB) Writes In-place page updates Sequential appends, later compaction Reads Predictable, one lookup path May check several levels (Bloom filters help) Best for Read-heavy, range queries Write-heavy, ingest Rule of thumb: replicate first, shard last; every shard multiplies operational work. CHAPTER 10 · CACHING & CONSISTENCY Caching Strategies That Actually Work THE IDEA Pick where the cache sits, how it fills and how it is invalidated. HOW IT WORKS 1 Request Request arrives 2 Check cache Look in cache 3 Miss: read DB Miss: load from DB 4 Populate cache Fill cache with TTL 5 Invalidate on write Delete on change REMEMBER Default to cache-aside with a TTL safety net. Beat stampedes: single-flight, jittered TTLs. State the staleness you accept, in seconds. DEEP DIVE Patterns PATTERN HOW IT WORKS USE WHEN Cache-aside App reads cache, on miss loads DB and fills cache Default choice; read-heavy data Read-through Cache itself loads from the source You want loading logic in one place Write-through Write to cache and DB together Reads must see fresh data Write-behind Write to cache, flush to DB later High write rate; can tolerate loss risk Refresh- Reload hot keys before they expire Predictable hot set, expensive ahead loads Failure modes to design for Stampede (thundering herd). A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB. Use single-flight locking, request coalescing, soft TTLs or jittered expiry. Penetration. Requests for keys that do not exist bypass the cache. Cache negative results briefly or use a Bloom filter. Avalanche. Many keys expire together. Add random jitter to TTLs. Hot key. One key overloads one cache node. Replicate it or add a small local (L1) cache. Stale data. Delete on write rather than update, and set a TTL as a safety net. collapse concurrent loads of the same key within one JVM. @Cacheable(cacheNames = "product", key = "#id", sync = true) public Product find(long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); } @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "product", key = "#p.id") public void update(Product p) { repo.save(p); } HARD TRUTH Cache invalidation is hard because the cache and the database are two systems updated non-atomically. Always state the staleness you accept, in seconds, for each cache.

CHAPTER 11 · CACHING & CONSISTENCY How Meta Reaches 99.99999999% Cache Consistency THE IDEA Measure inconsistency continuously instead of trying to prevent every race. HOW IT WORKS 1 DB write Database write happens 2 Invalidation event Event tells caches to drop it 3 Polaris checks caches Polaris verifies cache state 4 Re-check later if mismatch Re-check later before alarming 5 Trace explains why Tracing finds the race REMEMBER Define consistency as a measured number. Cheap detector + targeted tracer. Most mismatches are just in-flight events. DEEP DIVE Meta's caches sit in front of a huge database tier and are kept in sync by invalidation events flowing from the database. Races between concurrent writes, reads and invalidations can still leave a cache entry stale. Rather than assume perfection, Meta built a service to observe consistency. Polaris It consumes the same invalidation stream and, for each event, asks cache servers whether they now hold a stale value. To avoid hammering the database, it re-checks mismatches at growing intervals (minutes) before declaring a real inconsistency. Most apparent mismatches are just inflight events that resolve themselves. It treats a cache as a client of the database and defines consistency as “eventually reflects the latest write”, then reports a fraction of writes that stay inconsistent beyond a window. Finding the cause Polaris says that something is stale; a tracing library embedded in cache servers explains why. It records only the narrow time window in which a race could occur, for the affected keys, so the volume stays manageable. Engineers can then see the interleaving of events that caused the bug. TA K E AWAY Two ideas transfer to any system: define consistency as a measurable SLO, and pair a cheap detector with a targeted tracer so you can both notice and debug rare races. In your own services, a periodic reconciliation job that compares cache and DB samples is a small version of the same thing. 12 How AWS Lambda Works THE IDEA Fleets of workers running Firecracker microVMs, kept warm and fast to start. HOW IT WORKS 1 Invoke Function is called 2 Frontend routes request Front end accepts the call 3 Placement finds a worker Placement picks an environment 4 Worker runs microVM Firecracker microVM boots or restores 5 Function executes Your code runs REMEMBER microVMs give VM isolation at container speed. Cold starts: reuse, snapshots, lazy image loading. Java: SnapStart, native image, fewer beans. DEEP DIVE Lambda runs your function on demand, billing per invocation. Behind the simple API sits a set of cooperating services: a frontend that accepts invocations, a placement service that picks or creates an execution environment, and workers (physical hosts) that run it. Isolation with microVMs Many customers share a worker, so isolation must be strong. Each execution environment runs inside a Firecracker microVM: a minimal virtual machine that boots in a fraction of a second with a tiny memory footprint, giving VM-level isolation at near-container density. The cold start problem A cold start is the time to create an environment, download code, start the runtime and run your init code. Lambda attacks it in layers: Reuse. After a run, the environment is kept warm for later invocations, so later calls skip all setup. Snapshots. Initialised environments can be snapshotted and restored, rather than booted from scratch. For Java this is exposed as SnapStart. Lazy, deduplicated image loading. Container images are fetched in chunks on demand, and chunks shared across layers and customers are cached instead of re-downloaded. Provisioned concurrency keeps a number of environments pre-initialised if you need guaranteed low latency. Fault tolerance Control-plane state, such as which worker owns which environment, is kept in replicated, journaled stores so a failed component can be replaced without losing track of running work. FOR JAVA DEVELOPERS JVM cold starts are the weak spot. Reduce them with SnapStart, GraalVM native image, fewer or lazier beans (Spring Cloud Function, or Micronaut/Quarkus), and a lean dependency set. Beware of state captured in a snapshot: refresh connections, random seeds and credentials after restore.

13 How DNS Works THE IDEA A hierarchy of caches and delegations that turns names into addresses. HOW IT WORKS 1 Browser/OS cache Local caches first 2 Recursive resolver Resolver asks around 3 Root server Root points to the TLD 4 TLD server TLD points to the owner 5 Authoritative server Owner answers, TTL cached REMEMBER Hierarchy of delegations plus caches everywhere. TTL is your failover speed. Anycast and geo routing steer users. DEEP DIVE The Domain Name System is a distributed, hierarchical database. No single server knows everything; each knows whom to ask next, and almost every answer is cached. A lookup for api.example.com The browser and operating system check their caches. On a miss, the stub resolver asks a recursive resolver (your ISP, or 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8), which checks its own cache. The resolver asks a root server, which answers with the servers for the .com TLD. The TLD server answers with the authoritative name servers for example.com . The authoritative server returns the record. The resolver caches it for the record's TTL and returns it to the client. RECORD MEANING A / AAAA Name to IPv4 / IPv6 address CNAME Alias to another name NS Delegates a zone to name servers MX Mail routing TXT Arbitrary text (SPF, verification) Why architects care TTL is your failover speed. A 24-hour TTL means a bad record lingers; use 30–300 s for records you may change. DNS as a load balancer. Round-robin, weighted, latency-based and geo routing (Route steer traffic across regions, but clients cache, so it is coarse. Anycast lets many servers share one IP, so resolvers and CDNs reach the nearest one. JVM caching. The JVM can cache DNS results ( networkaddress.cache.ttl ); in cloud environments set a short value or endpoint changes will be ignored. Failure story: many big outages start with DNS, so review record changes like code.

14 Load Balancers, API Gateways and CDNs THE IDEA Three front-door layers that look similar but solve different problems. HOW IT WORKS 1 Client User asks 2 CDN (edge cache) Edge serves cached content 3 Load balancer Spread across healthy nodes 4 API gateway Auth, limits, routing 5 Services Business logic REMEMBER CDN caches; balancer spreads; gateway governs. L4 is fast; L7 can route by content. Version asset names; cache them forever. DEEP DIVE LAYER JOB EXAMPLES CDN Cache static and cacheable content near users; absorb traffic spikes; terminate TLS at the edge CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai Load Spread connections across healthy instances; health ALB/NLB, NGINX, Envoy, balancer checks HAProxy API Auth, rate limiting, routing, request shaping, API Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, gateway keys, versioning AWS API Gateway Load balancing L4 (TCP) is fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 (HTTP) can route by path, header or cookie. Algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted, consistent hash (for cache affinity). Least-connections copes better with uneven request cost. Health checks and connection draining make deploys and failures invisible to users. The balancer itself must not be a single point of failure: run it redundantly, across zones. CDN essentials and ETag . Use versioned asset names ( app.3f9a1c.js ) so you can cache for a year and never purge. Offload large file delivery to the CDN, with origin shielding to protect the backend. IN SPRING Spring Cloud Gateway gives you route predicates, filters, a Redis-backed RequestRateLimiter and Resilience4j circuit breaker filters. Keep business logic out of the gateway; it should stay a thin edge.

15 How Micro Frontends Work THE IDEA Splitting a web UI into independently deployable, team-owned slices. HOW IT WORKS 1 Shell app One thin app shell 2 Loads remote modules Remote slices loaded at runtime 3 Each team owns a slice Teams deploy independently 4 Shared design system Design system shared 5 Events between slices Slices talk via events REMEMBER Split by business domain, not tech layer. Share a design system, not business code. Worth it only with many autonomous teams. DEEP DIVE Micro frontends apply the microservice idea to the browser. Instead of one large singlepage app owned by many teams, the UI is composed from vertical slices that each own a business capability end to end: UI, backend-for-frontend and data. Composition options APPROACH HOW NOTES Build-time packages Slices published as npm packages Simple, but deploys are coupled Module Federation Shell loads remote bundles at runtime Independent deploys; shared dependency negotiation Web Components Slices are custom elements Framework-agnostic iframes Hard isolation Poor UX and routing; secure sandboxing Server-side / edge HTML assembled on the Fast first paint, good SEO includes server Rules that keep it sane Split by business domain, not by technical layer. Communicate through events and URLs, not shared global state. Share a design system, not business code, to keep the look consistent. Pair each slice with a backend-for-frontend so its API fits its UI. Agree on runtime contracts and test them (consumer-driven contracts). HONEST TRADE-OFF Micro frontends add bundle size, duplicated dependencies and operational overhead. They pay off with many autonomous teams and a mature platform. For a team of ten, a modular monolith frontend is usually the better design. 16 How Uber Finds Nearby Drivers THE IDEA Index the planet into cells, then search only the neighbouring cells. HOW IT WORKS 1 Driver pings location Driver sends GPS 2 Map to H3 cell Position becomes a cell id 3 Store cell → drivers Cell holds its drivers 4 Rider' s cell + ring Rider cell plus neighbours 5 Rank candidates Pick the best REMEMBER Turn 2D proximity into key lookups. Hexagons have equal-distance neighbours. Keep live positions in memory, not the main DB. DEEP DIVE Scanning every driver for each request is impossible. A geospatial index turns “who is near here?” into a few key lookups. H3: hexagonal hierarchical index Uber's open-source H3 divides the globe into hexagonal cells at 16 resolutions. Each cell has a 64-bit id. Hexagons have equidistant neighbours, so “within k rings” approximates a circle well, avoiding the corner-versus-edge distortions of squares. Each cell has a parent and children, so you can coarsen or refine resolution cheaply (bit operations on the id). Search = compute the rider's cell, take its gridDisk(k) neighbours, and read the drivers in those cells. Alternatives INDEX IDEA NOTE Geohash Interleaved lat/lon bits as a string prefix Simple; edge cases at cell borders Quadtree Recursively split space where dense Adaptive; harder to distribute S2 ( Google) Cells on a sphere along a Hilbert curve Used by Tinder and others H3 Hexagonal grid Best neighbour semantics PostGIS / Redis Spatial index in a DB Fine up to moderate scale GEO Operating it Drivers update location every few seconds. Keep live positions in memory (Redis or a stateful service) with a short TTL, not in the primary DB. Shard by cell id, with a consistent hash ring so cells can move between nodes. Pick resolution per use case: finer for dense cities, coarser for rural. Takeaway: turn a 2D proximity problem into a 1D key lookup.

17 How Uber Computes ETA THE IDEA A road graph, a fast shortest-path algorithm and live traffic. HOW IT WORKS 1 Map as graph Roads become a graph 2 Weights = travel time Edge weight = travel time 3 Fast routing structure Precompute to skip search work 4 Add live traffic Live traffic updates weights 5 Map-match GPS Snap noisy GPS to roads REMEMBER Too slow online? Do the work offline. ML corrects the routing baseline. HMM + Viterbi map-matching cleans GPS. DEEP DIVE The road network is a directed weighted graph: intersections are nodes, road segments are edges, and the weight is the predicted travel time. An ETA is the cost of the shortest path between two points. Why plain Dijkstra is not enough Dijkstra works, but exploring a continent-sized graph for every request is far too slow at Uber's request rate. The standard answer is preprocessing: spend effort offline to build a structure that makes each online query touch only a tiny part of the graph. Techniques in this family include graph partitioning, contraction hierarchies and A* with landmarks. Uber has described partitioning the graph and precomputing routes within and between partitions. Making weights realistic Edge weights come from live and historical traffic, usually per road segment and time of day. A model (often gradient-boosted trees or a neural network) can correct the raw routing estimate using features such as weather, events and time. The route engine gives a baseline; ML closes the gap. Map matching GPS points are noisy and jump off the road. Map matching snaps a sequence of points to the most likely path along the road graph. A Hidden Markov Model decoded with the Viterbi algorithm balances “close to the GPS reading” against “a plausible move from the previous road”. A Kalman filter smooths position and speed estimates. Clean matched traces feed both live ETA and the traffic data. TA K E AWAY When an algorithm is too slow online, move the work offline. When data is noisy, model the uncertainty instead of trusting a single reading.

18 How Tinder Handles Billions of Swipes THE IDEA Geo-index, key-value storage, streams for matching and defences against hot shards. HOW IT WORKS 1 Swipe User swipes 2 API gateway Gateway authenticates 3 Stream of swipes Swipe goes to a stream 4 Match service Match check consumer 5 WebSocket push Push over WebSocket REMEMBER Streams decouple swipes from matching. S2 cells for nearby search. Design for the hottest shard at peak. DEEP DIVE The workload is write-heavy and bursty: huge numbers of tiny events (a swipe is a few bytes) with a matching check on each. The design reflects that. Location search. Google S2 cells index users so “people near me” becomes a cell lookup. Key- value / document storage for profiles and relationships, which are accessed by id and need horizontal scale. Event streaming. Each swipe is published to a stream. A consumer checks whether the other person has already swiped right and, if so, writes a match. This decouples ingestion from matching. Change data capture propagates table changes to search indexes and analytics without dual writes. Real-time delivery. Matches and messages are pushed over WebSockets. Service mesh + API gateway to manage hundreds of microservices: mTLS, retries, timeouts and traffic policy outside application code. Hot shards Usage follows time zones, so one region's shards can go hot every evening. Mitigations in the playbook-style toolbox: Many small shards per server, so load can be rebalanced by moving shards, not splitting them. Caching absorbs read hot spots. Rate limiting caps write hot spots from abusive or buggy clients. Backoff with jitter on failures prevents retries from amplifying overload. TA K E AWAY Design for skew, not averages. The busiest shard at the busiest hour is the one that sets your capacity plan.

19 Real-Time Communication: Polling, SSE and WebSockets THE IDEA Choosing how the server tells the client something happened. HOW IT WORKS 1 Client connects Client connects 2 Server holds channel Server holds the channel 3 Event occurs Something changes 4 Server pushes Server pushes 5 Client acks / reconnects Client resumes on drop REMEMBER Server to client only? Use SSE. Two-way or gaming? WebSocket. Plan for reconnects, heartbeats, sequence numbers. DEEP DIVE TECHNIQUE DIRECTION COST USE WHEN Short polling Client asks repeatedly Many wasted requests Rare updates, simplicity Long polling Request held until data arrives Reconnect per event Fallback, old proxies Server-Sent Server → client, over Cheap, auto-reconnect, Feeds, notifications, Events HTTP text only progress WebSocket Full duplex Stateful connection per client Chat, games, collaboration gRPC streaming Bidirectional Needs HTTP/2 end to end Service-to-service Scaling stateful connections A WebSocket pins a client to one server, so you need a way to find it. Keep a connection registry (user id → node) in Redis, or broadcast through a pub/sub backbone (Redis, Kafka, NATS) that every node subscribes to. Sticky sessions help the handshake, but never rely on them for correctness. Expect clients to drop. Use heartbeats, reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and sequence numbers so a client can resume from the last event it saw. Keep per-connection memory small; one node can hold hundreds of thousands of idle connections if tuned (file descriptors, buffers). IN SPRING Spring MVC supports SseEmitter ; Spring WebFlux returns Flux<ServerSentEvent> and scales idle connections better on few threads. For WebSocket use STOMP over a broker relay (RabbitMQ) or a plain handler for custom protocols. Default to SSE when you only push server to client. P A R T 6 Reliability & Payments Make operations safe to retry, calls safe to fail and events safe to replay. 20 How Stripe Prevents Double Payments THE IDEA Idempotency keys turn a dangerous retry into a harmless one. HOW IT WORKS 1 2 3 4 5 Client sends key Unique key per operation Server looks up key Check the store New? process & store New: do it, save the result Seen? return savedExpire after 24h result Seen: replay the saved result Keys expire after a window REMEMBER Retry-safe by design: same key, same effect. Store the key and the change in one transaction. Reject same key with a different payload. DEEP DIVE Networks fail ambiguously: a timeout does not tell you whether the charge happened. If the client retries a plain POST /charges , the customer may be billed twice. An idempotent operation can be repeated with the same effect as doing it once. The idempotency-key protocol The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per logical operation and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. The server looks the key up in a store. If it is new, the server records it, performs the work and saves the response (status and body) against the key. On a retry with the same key, the server returns the saved response without running the work again. If the same key arrives with a different payload, reject it, because this signals a client bug. Keys expire after a window (Stripe documents 24 hours), after which they can be reused. Details that matter Atomicity. The key record and the business change must commit together, ideally in one database transaction. A unique constraint on the key makes concurrent duplicates fail safely. In-flight requests. Mark a key processing; a concurrent duplicate waits or gets 409 . Server errors. Roll back on failure so the key does not store a half-done result. Downstream calls (the card network) need their own idempotency or a reconciliation job. // Sketch: Spring filter/aspect around POST handlers Optional prior = store.find(key, userId); if (prior.isPresent()) { if (!prior.get().requestHash().equals(hash(body))) throw new ConflictException(); return prior.get().toResponse(); } if (!store.tryClaim(key, userId, hash(body))) // unique index on (userId, key) throw new InProgressException(); // -> 409 try { var resp = handler.proceed(); store.complete(key, resp); return resp; } catch (Exception e) { store.release(key); throw e; } ALSO REMEMBER Retries from clients should use exponential backoff with jitter, covered in the next chapter. Idempotency makes retries safe; backoff makes them polite.

21 Retries, Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Rate Limits THE IDEA The four defences that stop one slow dependency from taking everything down. HOW IT WORKS 1 Set timeout Every call gets a deadline 2 Retry with backoff Few attempts, jittered delay 3 Open circuit if failing Fail fast when unhealthy 4 Fallback / shed load Degrade gracefully 5 Rate limit callers Cap what callers may send REMEMBER Timeout everything; retry only idempotent calls. Backoff with jitter prevents retry storms. Bulkheads isolate failures. DEEP DIVE Timeouts Every network call needs a timeout. Without one, a slow dependency ties up threads until your own service is the one that fails. Set a budget per request and propagate a deadline downward so inner calls never outlive the outer one. Retries Retry only idempotent operations and only transient errors (timeouts, 503, 429), never 4xx validation errors. Use exponential backoff with jitter: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)) . Jitter spreads retries so clients do not all return in lockstep. Cap attempts and total time. Retries at several layers multiply (3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls), so retry at one layer. Circuit breaker Tracks failures; when the failure rate crosses a threshold it opens and fails fast for a cooldown period, then half-opens to probe with a few trial calls. This gives the dependency room to recover and gives callers a fast, predictable error. Bulkheads and load shedding Isolate resources per dependency (separate thread pools or semaphores) so one failing service cannot exhaust the pool. Under overload, reject low-priority work early rather than slowing everything down. Rate limiting algorithms ALGORITHM BEHAVIOUR NOTE Fixed window Count per interval Simple; burst at boundaries Sliding window Smooth count over time More memory/accuracy Token bucket Refill at rate r, burst up to b Most common; allows bursts Leaky bucket Constant outflow Smooths traffic @CircuitBreaker(name = "payments", fallbackMethod = "queueForLater") @Retry(name = "payments") // resilience4j: maxAttempts, exponential backoff + jitter @TimeLimiter(name = "payments") public CompletableFuture charge(ChargeRequest r) { ... } TRADE-OFF Aggressive retries during an outage create a retry storm that prevents recovery. Prefer a retry budget (e.g. at most 10% extra traffic) over a fixed count.

22 Event-Driven Reliability: Outbox, Saga and Exactly-Once THE IDEA How to change a database and publish an event without losing or duplicating either. HOW IT WORKS 1 Write DB + outbox row Business row and outbox row 2 Relay reads outbox Relay reads the outbox 3 Publish to Kafka Event reaches Kafka 4 Consumers dedupe Handlers ignore duplicates 5 Saga compensates on failure Compensate if a step fails REMEMBER Outbox fixes the dual-write problem. Delivery is at-least-once; make consumers idempotent. Saga = local transactions + compensations. DEEP DIVE The dual-write problem Saving to a database and then publishing to a broker are two separate operations. If the service crashes between them, you have a change with no event, or an event for a change that rolled back. Transactional outbox Write the business row and an outbox row in the same local transaction. A relay then publishes outbox rows to the broker, either by polling or by change data capture (Debezium reading the database log). Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent: store processed event ids, or make the handler naturally repeatable (upserts). Delivery semantics GUARANTEE MEANING HOW At-most-once May lose, never duplicates Fire and forget At-least-once Never loses, may duplicate Retry + idempotent consumers Exactly-once Duplicates have no effect Idempotence, or Kafka transactions within (effect) Kafka “Exactly-once” across a broker and an external database is really at-least-once plus idempotent processing. Kafka transactions give atomic read-process-write only between Kafka topics. Saga A business transaction spanning services (order, payment, inventory) cannot use one ACID transaction. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action (refund, release stock) run if a later step fails. Choreography lets services react to each other's events; orchestration uses a coordinator that drives the steps and is easier to reason about. Ordering and partitions Kafka orders events only within a partition; key by aggregate id so all events of one order stay together. Use a dead-letter topic for poison messages and bounded retries with backoff. Plan for consumer lag and rebalances as first-class operational signals. the same method if loss matters. 23 Back-of-the-Envelope Numbers THE IDEA Order-of-magnitude figures that make capacity estimates quick. HOW IT WORKS 1 Estimate users Users 2 Requests/sec Per second 3 Data/day Per day 4 Storage/year Per year 5 Add headroom Peak and spare room REMEMBER 1M requests/day is about 12 per second. Design for 2 to 5 times average peak. Memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 us, cross-continent ~100 ms. DEEP DIVE OPERATION APPROX. LATENCY L1 cache reference ~1 ns Main memory reference ~100 ns SSD random read ~100 µs Round trip in same data centre ~0.5 ms HDD seek ~10 ms Cross-continent round trip ~100–150 ms Handy conversions 1 day ≈ 86,400 s, so 1 M requests/day ≈ 12 req/s average. Peak is typically 2–5× the average; design for peak. 1KB×1M=1GB.1MB×1M=1TB. A single well-tuned database node handles low thousands of simple writes/s; an inmemory cache handles 100k+ ops/s per node. Availability: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h downtime/year; 99.99% ≈ 53 min; 99.999% ≈ 5 min. Worked example A service with 50 M daily users, 20 requests each: 1 B requests/day ≈ 11,600 req/s average, ~40k req/s at 3.5× peak. At 2 KB per response, that is about 80 MB/s of egress at peak. These figures are estimates; state your assumptions aloud and refine them. U S E Numbers here are rough, widely quoted approximations. Their value is the order of magnitude, not the digits.

24 Choosing the Right Tool: Decision Tables THE IDEA A compact map from requirement to technique. HOW IT WORKS 1 State requirement Name the requirement 2 Find constraint Find the constraint 3 Pick pattern Choose a pattern 4 Name trade-off Say the cost REMEMBER Never present one option. Money needs strong consistency; feeds can be eventual. Say what would make you change your mind. DEEP DIVE IF YOU NEED… REACH FOR… WATCH OUT FOR Fast repeated reads Cache-aside (Redis) Stampedes, staleness Safe client retries Idempotency keys Atomic key storage Decouple producers and Kafka / queue Ordering, duplicates, lag consumers DB change + event atomically Transactional outbox + CDC At-least-once delivery Multi-service business Saga Compensation design transaction Scale reads Replicas, cache, CDN Replication lag Scale writes / size Sharding Cross-shard queries, resharding Even load on elastic nodes Consistent hashing Hot keys Proximity search H3 / S2 / geohash Cell-boundary effects Push to browsers SSE, WebSocket Connection state, reconnects Protect a dependency Timeouts, breaker, bulkhead Retry storms Large binary data Object store + pre-signed URLs Consistency of metadata Stateless auth across services JWT (short-lived) + refresh Revocation Quick consistency picks Money, inventory, identity: strong consistency, single-leader or consensus. Feeds, counters, recommendations: eventual consistency is fine. User sees their own writes: read-your-writes via sticky reads or version tokens. 25 A Framework for Any System Design Question THE IDEA Seven steps that keep a long discussion on track. HOW IT WORKS 1 Clarify Clarify 5 Deep dive Deep dive 2 Estimate Estimate 6 Failure & scale Break it 3 API & data model API and data 7 Trade-offs Trade-offs 4 High-level design Big picture REMEMBER Requirements and numbers before boxes. Start simple; add components only when forced. Always ask: what dies, and what is stale? DEEP DIVE Clarify requirements. Functional scope, users, read/write ratio, latency, consistency and availability targets. Estimate scale. Requests per second, storage, bandwidth. Define APIs and the data model. Entities, keys, access patterns. Sketch the high-level architecture. Clients, edge, services, data stores, async paths. Deep -dive the hardest one or two components (hot path, hot keys, consistency). Probe failure and scaling. What breaks first? Replication, retries, back-pressure, multi- region. Summarise trade-offs and what you would build in version one versus later. Questions to ask yourself at each box What happens if this node, zone or dependency dies? What is the bottleneck at 10× load? Where can data be stale, and for how long? How do I observe it: metrics, logs, traces, SLOs? What is the simplest design that meets the stated need? SIMPLEST FIRST Begin with a monolith and one database; add components only when a stated requirement forces them. Each box you add is something you must operate.
